key: G major, ending in E major
intro: The fourth movement of Mahler’s Fourth Symphony, marked Sehr behaglich, is a setting of ‘Das himmlische Leben’ for soprano, describing a heaven where Saint Martha cooks, Peter fishes and the saints make music. The orchestra includes sleigh bells, and the text describes the slaughter of a lamb.

sections.mNote: A tune above muted violas and cellos

cues.title: Opening: clarinet, horn and harp
cues.text: A clarinet opens over horn, harp and muted violas and cellos. The violins and double basses rest. Mahler marked the music Sehr behaglich (very comfortable) and told the conductor to accompany the singer with extreme discretion.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, printed p. 328: opening instrumentation, Sehr behaglich and the note to the conductor above the movement. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening vocal entry, soprano
cues.text: The soprano begins with the pleasures of heaven, where no earthly commotion reaches. At her entry Mahler marked the part Mit kindlich heiterem Ausdruck; durchaus ohne Parodie, asking for a childlike, cheerful voice and ruling out parody. Harp and lightly plucked strings accompany her.
cues.evidence: Full score, opening vocal entry: Mit kindlich heiterem Ausdruck; durchaus ohne Parodie. The poem is from Des Knaben Wunderhorn; text and discussion at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fliessend, “We lead an angelic life”
cues.text: The tempo quickens at Fliessend (flowing) for “We lead an angelic life”. The rhythm livens further at “we dance and leap, we hop and sing”.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide describes the quickening at the text about dancing, leaping and hopping, marked Fliessend: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sleigh bells and second stanza
cues.text: The sleigh bells return between verses. The second stanza moves to E minor, and the child describes the food of heaven: John leads out a lamb, Herod waits for it, and Saint Luke slaughters the ox.
cues.evidence: Full score, second orchestral interlude and second vocal stanza; German text and English translation at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . E-minor second stanza: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second verse, oboe and bass clarinet
cues.text: The second verse has a new melody. As the text turns to the slaughter of lamb and ox, an oboe imitates a sheep’s bleat and a bass clarinet an ox’s bellow. The sleigh bells have stopped.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide describes the oboe and bass clarinet imitations and the new soprano melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third stanza, return of first melody
cues.text: Another passage for bells leads to the return of the first-verse melody. In the third stanza, herbs and vegetables grow in heaven’s garden and fruit is free. Deer and hares run into the kitchen, Saint Martha is to be the cook, and the orchestral accompaniment quickens.
cues.evidence: Third stanza of the Wunderhorn poem and its returning first-verse melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Full score, third vocal stanza and its quickening accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition of the song, 1892
cues.text: Mahler finished the voice-and-piano version of Das himmlische Leben on 10 February 1892 and completed the orchestral version on 12 March. Years later he built the Fourth Symphony around it as the finale.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s work history dates the piano version to 10 February 1892 and the orchestral version to 12 March: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: Final section in E major
cues.text: The last sleigh-bell interruption fades. At rehearsal 12 (Tempo I, Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss), flute and cor anglais play a new melody in E major above harp triplets and muted strings, while the soprano rests. The symphony ends in E major.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 349, rehearsal 12: Tempo I, Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss; flute and cor anglais, harp triplets and muted strings. Final section in E major: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s recording, Leipzig, 1905
cues.text: On 9 November 1905 in Leipzig, Mahler recorded a piano version of this finale on the Welte-Mignon reproducing piano. The Mahler Foundation lists it first among the symphony’s historical recordings.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page lists “09-11-1905 Leipzig. Gustav Mahler. Symphony No. 4 – Movement 4 … Welte-Mignon” first among the historical recordings: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-history/

cues.title: Fourth stanza, soprano
cues.text: The soprano takes up the E-major tune. The text tells of heavenly music that surpasses any on earth, with eleven thousand virgins dancing and Saint Ursula laughing. The voice sings over steady triplets in the harp, and there is no grand final chorus.
cues.evidence: Fourth stanza of the Wunderhorn poem, full score, printed pp. 350–353; text at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Saint Ursula, rehearsal 14
cues.text: At “Sanct Ursula selbst dazu lacht” (Saint Ursula herself laughs at it), the music slows and holds a pause before the next phrase. In 1901 Mahler described the saint as presiding over the Adagio with a smile.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 351: Sanct Ur-sula selbst dazu lacht! with riten., a fermata and kurz a tempo at rehearsal 14: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf . Mahler’s 1901 description of St Ursula presiding over the Adagio: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cecilia and her relations
cues.text: The poem names Cecilia and her relations as splendid court musicians, whose angelic voices bring everything to life with joy. Mahler keeps the accompaniment small. Rocking harp notes, soft strings and wind phrases surround the soprano’s final words.
cues.evidence: Final lines of the Wunderhorn poem: Cäcilia mit ihren Verwandten sind treffliche Hofmusikanten; full score, printed pp. 352–353.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars, harp
cues.text: After the soprano finishes, cor anglais and bass clarinet fade over low strings. The harp plays alone between the held notes. Mahler marks it sich Zeit lassen (take time) before the last chord in E major.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 353: final instrumental bars, harp sich Zeit lassen, morendo and sustained cello and bass ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: First soprano entry after the prelude
transitions.how: The prelude, led by the clarinet, closes in G major. The soprano enters above harp and plucked strings, and soft wind phrases surround the vocal line. Mahler asked for a cheerful, childlike expression and kept the accompaniment light.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 328–330, prelude and first vocal entry.

transitions.title: Sleigh bells follow the G-major refrain
transitions.to: B · Sleigh bells before the butcher’s verse
transitions.how: The first verse ends with a soft, hymn-like refrain over muted strings and horns. Sleigh bells and high woodwind break in, and the strings play col legno. The soprano then begins a new melody in E minor for the verse about the slaughter of the lamb.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first refrain, sleigh-bell interlude and second verse; movement guide and text: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: The first melody returns after the bells
transitions.from: B · Sleigh bells before the butcher’s verse
transitions.to: A′ · Bells, then first theme returns
transitions.how: The hymn-like close of the second verse is followed by another sleigh-bell interruption. The soprano then sings the melody of the first verse again for the garden stanza, and winds and strings return to its lighter accompaniment. Faster figures soon follow for the lines about running animals and swimming fish.
transitions.evidence: Full score, second refrain, orchestral interlude and third verse; https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: Final sleigh-bell interlude
transitions.from: A′ · Bells, then first theme returns
transitions.how: The verse about Saint Martha ends in a broad refrain. Sleigh bells, triangle, winds and strings enter once more. The interlude is short and the scoring thins out before rehearsal 12, where the music moves to a new key and a softer tune.
transitions.evidence: Full score, third refrain and final bell interlude before rehearsal 12.

transitions.title: E major at rehearsal 12
transitions.to: C · Flute and cor anglais, E major
transitions.how: The bells and forceful wind figures die away. At rehearsal 12 the music moves to E major. The harp plays a triplet accompaniment, and flute and cor anglais begin the last tune. Muted strings join under the marking Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss (very tender and mysterious to the end).
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 349, rehearsal 12: Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss.

transitions.title: The soprano takes the E-major tune
transitions.from: C · Flute and cor anglais, E major
transitions.to: C′ · Soprano melody in E major
transitions.how: The soprano enters with the E-major music the winds have already played. Harp triplets continue beneath muted strings and soft wind chords. The voice takes over the orchestral melody for the song of heaven’s musicians, and the bells do not interrupt again.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 349–351, orchestral introduction and fourth vocal stanza.

transitions.title: Instrumental postlude after the soprano’s close
transitions.from: C′ · Soprano melody in E major
transitions.to: Coda · harp continues after the voice
transitions.how: The soprano finishes over E-major harmony. Cor anglais and bass clarinet continue the line, then fade out with the horns. Above sustained cellos and basses the harp notes slow down. On printed p. 353 of the full score the harpist is marked sich Zeit lassen before the final chord.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 353: instrumental postlude and harp direction sich Zeit lassen.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, IV. Das himmlische Leben, full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: Fourth movement, printed pp. 328–353, rehearsal figures 1–15: four vocal stanzas, sleigh-bell interludes and the E-major ending.

timeline.note: A clarinet and a horn with harp, over muted violas and cellos; violins and basses rest.
Oboes, cor anglais, bass clarinet and bassoons add soft phrases; the basses pluck.
The soprano sings over clarinets, harp and discreet pizzicato strings.
Flutes and clarinets quicken with the voice as the text turns to dancing and singing.
Muted strings and soft horns accompany the hymn-like close of the verse about Saint Peter.
Sleigh bells, triangle and woodwinds with bells up play in the minor; the strings strike with the wood of the bow.
The soprano sings the lamb’s verse to a new melody, with oboe and bass clarinet answering.
The first melody returns for the verses about the garden’s herbs and fruit.
The tempo quickens. Strings and woodwinds play swirling figures, with brief sleigh bells, for running game and darting fish.
The refrain grows louder for Saint Martha the cook, then quieter again.
Sleigh bells and triangle ring with fortissimo winds and strings, then fade to pp.
Flute and cor anglais introduce the E-major tune over harp triplets and muted strings.
The soprano takes the new tune over muted strings, harp triplets and soft winds.
The harp plays triplets beneath the muted strings and the voice.
Cor anglais and bass clarinet fade; the harp slows; cellos and basses hold a soft sustained note.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
